turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry doctor, we got stuck in traffic from the other side of town, and he was getting restless in the car.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): That is quite all right, please sit. So, tell me, what brings you in today?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): My ankle. I twisted it.
[SEG0004] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yesterday evening, doctor, at cricket practice. He jumped for a catch and landed all wrong, and the left ankle twisted under him.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ah, I see. How has it been since then? Tell me in your own words.
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): It is paining. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0007] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Pain is there from yesterday itself, and the swelling came within an hour. He can walk, but limping is there, and it pains when he puts the foot down.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Outer side or inner side, where does it feel worse?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Outside. I think.
[SEG0010] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Outer side, just below the ankle bone. That is what he kept saying at home also.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): When it happened, did you hear any pop, or a crack?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0013] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, there was no cracking sound. He just sat on the pitch and held it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. And now, can he take four steps on it, even if it hurts?
[SEG0015] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes, he walked in from the auto. Slowly, with pain, but he is putting weight, not hopping.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): It hurts when I walk.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness, or pins and needles, in the toes?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about fever? Shivering, or feeling very hot?
[SEG0020] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. He ate his dinner and was chatting, only the ankle was the issue.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has this ankle been hurt before? Any fracture, any plaster cast, anything of that sort?
[SEG0022] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing. First time only.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, good. Any medicine he has reacted badly to? Rash, swelling, trouble breathing?

[SEG0024] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. Ibuprofin. When he was small, around five years, we gave ibuprofin syrup for a fever and his lips swelled up, and red itchy rashes came all over the body. The child specialist said never give that again.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I am glad you remembered. We will keep away from ibuprofen, Brufen, and the other pain tablets in that family. Has he taken paracetamol, Crocin, without any trouble?
[SEG0026] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Many times, for fever. No problem at all with Crocin.
[SEG0027] person_3 (PATIENT): It tastes bad.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ha, most syrups do. The nurse has noted the readings here. Blood pressure is one oh nine over seventy-seven. Pulse, err, it looks like ninety-four... no, sorry, I misread the slip, it is eighty-eight.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Last time, in March, the pressure was one-forty over ninety, but he had fever then, so I am not using that figure today.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come, hop up, I will be gentle. You tell me if it is too much.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): There is swelling over the outer left ankle, a bit puffy, no big bruise. I am pressing behind the outer ankle bone and the inner one now.
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. Not the bone. The soft part. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0033] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was crying with it in the night, but since morning he is a little better.

[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, the soft tissue on the outer side is tender. Along the back of both malleoli I am not finding bony tenderness. Let me check the foot, the navicular area and the base of the little toe bone.
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): That is okay.
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): No tenderness over the navicular, and none at the fifth metatarsal base. And he has just taken four steps, limping, but bearing weight the whole way.
[SEG0037] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): In the waiting room also he wanted to keep standing. The coach has already phoned about Sunday's match, can you believe.

[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): The match will have to wait, I am sorry. Let me explain how I am deciding. Using the Ottawa rules, the pain is in the ankle, but there is no bony tenderness behind either malleolus, no tenderness on the navicular or the fifth metatarsal base, and he can bear weight for four steps. Clinically I do not think there is a fracture. My working impression is a sprain of the outer ankle ligaments.
[SEG0039] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So no X-ray today?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. If the swelling increases, or if he cannot put weight on the foot, then we will do an ankle X-ray. If it is settling, we can spare him that.
[SEG0041] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And at home, what all should we do? Sitting still is not his habit, I am warning you.

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Rest is the main medicine, no cricket and no running until the pain settles. Keep the leg elevated on a pillow when he sits or sleeps. Ice inside a cloth for about fifteen minutes, three or four times a day, never straight on the skin.
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): No cricket? Umm.
[SEG0044] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I will speak to the coach. For the pain, a tablet? I know not to give Brufen.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): Quite right, no Brufen, no ibuprofen, and no diclofenac. Paracetamol, that is Crocin, five hundred milligrams, one tablet by mouth, up to three times a day if the pain is there. Leave four hours between doses, and not more than three tablets in the day.
[SEG0046] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Five hundred, he is fourteen only. Is that not a big dose?
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): At fourteen, five hundred milligrams is quite a proper dose. If the pain is only mild, you can skip a dose, no need to give it round the clock.
[SEG0048] person_1 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Do we fix a review, or come only if it is not settling?

[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): If he is not walking more comfortably in five days, come back and see me. Earlier than that if the swelling suddenly jumps up. Otherwise rest should carry him through. You were right to bring him.

spec.situation: Young player who twisted the ankle yesterday; swelling, can bear weight with pain; doctor applies Ottawa rules aloud, no X-ray unless it worsens; rest and elevation advice.

traps.happens: The doctor asks about drug reactions. Variants (use ONE per encounter): (a) the patient says 'No, never, I have taken penicillin and everything' (no allergy); (b) the patient is unsure ('maybe the antibiotic or the painkiller, nobody told me which'); (c) a real allergy with the reaction described; (d) allergies are never asked.
traps.label_rule: (a) NO allergy entry: negative_findings 'Allergies' absent. (b) allergy with status uncertain, the substance as described, the reaction if said, plus an allergy_uncertain uncertainty. (c) allergy with the reaction. (d) nothing at all. NEVER list a medicine the patient has taken without a reaction as an allergy, and the plan must not prescribe a drug of a recorded allergy's family.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: Doctor says "no big bruise"; large bruise absent is implied, but size wording differs.

omissions.text: Mechanism of injury: left ankle twisted under him after he jumped for a catch and landed awkwardly at cricket practice yesterday evening.
Limping was present despite being able to walk and bear weight.
Negative finding asked and answered: no shivering or feeling very hot along with no fever.
Ibuprofen allergy history included prior advice from a child specialist to never give it again.
Doctor explicitly advised to avoid diclofenac as well as ibuprofen/Brufen because of the NSAID allergy history.
Paracetamol should be used only if pain is present and can be skipped if pain is mild; it does not need to be given around the clock.
Examination/history detail: pain was not over the bone but over the soft part on the outer side.
Clinical plan nuance: no X-ray today because clinically fracture was not suspected under Ottawa ankle rules; X-ray can be spared if it is settling.
